description:
A Romano-Celtic temple situated within a large open precinct in the northwestern part of the town positioned adjacent to the town forum. The structure consists of a central inner chamber, or cella, surrounded by a 2.8-meter-wide ambulatory. The temple was likely roofed with ceramic tiles and may have featured carved stone architectural embellishments.

The excavation revealed a remarkably well-preserved tessellated floor within the ambulatory, located only 0.3 meters below the modern ground surface. This floor was composed of whitish limestone tesserae and showed evidence of extensive repairs using smaller pieces of terracotta tile. the pottery assemblage suggested a earliest date of late 3rd CE, and a coin from the House of Theodosius (AD 388–402) discovered lying directly on the floor surface provided strong evidence that the temple remained in active use into the early 5th century. Despite its late survival, the building eventually underwent systematic robbing, with its walls largely dismantled to their foundations.
